title: Estimating how many days before you don't need my animation skills anymore...
author: piXelicidio
selftext:
The fact that it could understand the initial pose, follow the request, and move the character was actually impressive. Even if it never gets AAA quality, I guess many of you will accept it at some point and make the funny animations a feature of your game.

I'm not a professional animator, and never wanted to be one. I just know how to modestly animate my characters using 3ds Max and the ancient Biped system, very quickly.

The main problem you/we will face with these AI approaches is the feedback and iteration. With every little fix and update, you are at risk of losing a lot of tokens without a guaranteed result. Also, the dependency we start experiencing when working with coding agents for too long sometimes makes you blind to old, conventional ways that could be even cheaper, easier, or even free.

replies.author: Nemo121121
replies.body:
The problem is most people are extrapolating general AI improving at a linear rate when capability appears to be following a logarithmic growth pattern.

Humans are really, really bad at understanding and extrapolating logarithmic growth. If you say it is 10 years away then it is probably really just 1 year away. I'd suggest that 1 year from now general (non-specialised ) AI models will be able to animate to a degree which is fully acceptable for indie games and a year after that at a level which is fully acceptable for AAA games.

Logarithmic progression is progression at a rate the human brain is not evolutionarily adapted to understand and/or extrapolate.

replies.author: aberroco
replies.body:
Seems to me it's more of logistic growth pattern. First artificial neural networks were barely able to recognize letters or words. Then came transformers and LLMs and progress did appeared logarithmic. And for a couple years just throwing more compute produced ever better results. Now... Yeah, the frontier models do work better, but it's not nearly enough, they still produce mostly slop and each new model offers marginal improvements. And most of development now goes into proper harnesses and compute optimizations. That is the typical logistic function. As the technology develops and it's a totally new field with everything unknown it starts slowly, then it matures, develops exponentially, as more and more low hanging fruits are becomes apparent. But Eventually there's no more such fruits left and the technology comes to a plateau.

Unless some new groundbreaking paper comes out with some new approach, I don't think LLMs would be any real threat to human professionals. And it's impossible to say when (or even if) such new research would come out. Could be a year, could be a decade, could be a century, could be never. Though, since we have human brains, the latter is most likely excluded.

replies.author: LinkesAuge
replies.body:
Mate, just in the last \~9 month coding abilities have massively improved for LLMs.

It is why SWEs went form AI assisted tab completion to generating 90%+ of code with AI agents and maybe not even reading/reviewing all of that.

To say there were marginal improvements is just insane. Astra for example is a giant step in visual capabilities. There are now benchmarks showing it has better spatial understanding than the human average. I have even seen a benchmark for object recognition and annotation where it now outperforms humans in speed, cost(!) and quality, ie it is now cheaper to let Astra do it than hire a dude in India to annotate images.

The same is true in mathematics. There have been massive jumps in capability. Two years ago it was college level. Last year it could compete at a high lvel in math comps and now in the recent months/weeks we have models that solve top of the line open problems in mathematics.  
That is NOT a gradual or linear change in capabilities..

The same could be said for video models and also 3d AI models.

Will AI models at some point plateau? Sure, there are still physical limits the world imposes on us but I think it is easy to underestimate how much room there is still left to go.  


PS: Another new threshold Astra has broken is reverse engineering from binaries. It can do that now at an extremely high level, certainly higher than any human would be able to in any reasonable time. It is already "superhuman" in that area.

replies.author: aberroco
replies.body:
\> not even reading/reviewing all of that

That's not SWE, that's vibe-coders. Good luck trying to make a proper non-hyper-casual game with that. Because it hits hard ceiling of bad code, where each bug fixed takes daily quota of tokens and makes two or more new bugs, and a basic sprite rendering makes a 5090 sweat at barely 60fps with freezes.

\> there are still physical limits the world imposes on us

I'm talking about other kind of limits. The same kind that stopped convolutional neural networks (image classifiers) growth - the hidden layers number to performance peaked at about 12 layers and after that the results get worse, until a new approach was invented. Or the kind that stopped regular perceptron-line of neural networks, with similar kind of problem - more layers make the network harder and longer to train while producing similar or worse results. LLMs in particular can't think, they can't remember stuff, the best they have is the input tokens they produced on previous iteration, and a harness/system prompt that tells them to reason before writing an answer. Reasoning is not thinking. It looks similar, but just like a photo looks similar to the physical world where the photo was taken. So lack of these two properties might be an obstacle, or it might be a brick wall. I'd say, that yeah, most likely when AI would truly have both of these, that would be AGI and potentially more capable than humans. But quite possible it would also have it's own brick wall.

Either way, what I see is that the code produced by Fable 5.1 is marginally better than by, say, Opus 4, or GPT 4. It's coupled better, it's accompanied by testing and stuff, so what harness instructs to do. But the code itself is still just as crappy. Given an opportunity, it shits on me dozens of classes and interfaces, 80% of which are absolutely make no sense to exist and only make the codebase overly complicated and perform terribly. It's still a junior level code, even if the tasks the code performs are lead level and the knowledge it takes to write is PhD or weeks of googling and research level. In other words - it's ocean wide and puddle deep.

replies.author: piXelicidio
replies.body:
Maybe some are out of the loop, but existing 3D/animation generation services are specialized models. Many of them actually borrow heavily from 3D scanning, photogrammetry, and computer vision algorithms that existed long before the current AI boom; they just generate multi-angle images and run reconstruction math on top, without really understanding what they are doing.  
  
What you see with recent LLMs is different. In those demos it is operating Blender directly, and in my case it is writing MaxScript to set the raw animation keys on the bones. The extraordinary part isn't a polished visual right now, but the fact that a general model has enough spatial and motion reasoning to actually control DCC software programmatically.

replies.author: piXelicidio
replies.body:
I work with 3ds Max, I instructed GPT-6 Astra the following steps:  
\- Make a script that inspect my rig initial state (bone orientations, positions) and output it to a text file.  
\- Analyze the text file. (This I believe will help to create a better starting point and avoid many execution fails)  
\- Then create a second script that will set the animation keys to my creature to achieve an attack animation with two hands and one step forward.

After a few syntax errors, the script did the job. Didn't asked for any further fine tuning.

The other examples you see around with Blender are using the Blender MCP for Codex and I don't think it would need anything else.

replies.author: piXelicidio
replies.body:
You know what is funny? Even if current GenAI doesn't deliver, it still manages to redirect a lot of attention and budgets away from traditional offers. Many developers, especially beginners whose entire workflow is centered around AI agents, tend to stay on that track and look to AI services first instead of buying from or hiring artists, often without even calculating and comparing the actual cost and effort.

There is also that common mindset: "Right now it is not great, but in a few months it will be amazing." So they drop money on a full year's subscription, and then there is no budget left for stock assets or freelancers.

I can see AI here not necessarily only as a text to result tool, but imagine a designer working with a programmer to actually enhance the design tools, so the designer will do only a basic concept of a rigging or animation, some basic input given in the tool and the AI does the tedious works in between that costs time and is not pleasant for some/most anyway. A lot of ai people keep thinking in terms of how long until x job is fully replaced when they should just think in terms of how long before ai becomes a foundational assisting tool for job x. 

Animation is one of those subjective things that an AI physically will never get 100 percent right. It can get general action and shapes just fine but for every project a human will have to fine tune it for their specific needs that fall outside the AI training data.  Like this post for example - gpt generate the first one the you edit it to get the second one. Thats what most workflows will evolve into

comments.author: ZAPcon_64
comments.body:
I haven't tried this yet as I haven't needed a lot of animations for my project at the moment, but I am curious of what all workflows are possible. 

For instance, starting by having the AI ONLY generate the main key frames for the animation, then going over those with a human hand to tune them more specifically, THEN having the AI complete the rest of the animation without altering the core key frames.

I also wonder how well it can add key poses from reference images. For instance, take a video of you performing the full attack yourself, break out the key poses and draw over them with a stick figure to show the skeleton, then feed that to Astra and see if it can create those base key frames in the animation before continuing with refinements...  

Looking forward to playing around with this in the near future to see what kind of workflows are possible.
